stances.claim: Aging is governed by genetic programming as an upper limit, but heredity is 'overtaken by better nutrition, regular sleep, friendly doctors, modern medicine, and healthy lifestyle.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Quotes psychiatrist friend Cornelio Banaag Jr., then validates the framework through his own family longevity data.
stances.confidence: high -- adopts and personalizes the medical framing

stances.claim: Continual brain use through learning, socializing online, and spiritual practice keeps neurotransmitters active and telomeres long; 'use it or lose it' because 'old dogs can still learn new tricks.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Translates neurobiology into folk maxim for general readers.

stances.claim: Retirement is not withdrawal but redirection -- 'merely a change of tires to embark on new journeys' -- and post-judicial life as independent director, philanthropist, and writer is structurally similar to judicial work in its requirement of independence.
stances.rhetorical_move: Frames the second career as faithful continuation of the first.

stances.claim: Faithful service ('owing fidelity to the corporations I serve as separate legal entities, not to the owners') is the carried-over standard from judicial service to corporate directorship.
stances.rhetorical_move: Imports judicial-independence framing into board service.

notable_anecdotes.description: Helped raise P200 million to retrofit, strengthen, and redecorate the Manila Cathedral; set up FLP scholarships, professorial chairs, and rewards for excellent dissertations -- works he 'did not know I could' accomplish in retirement.
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Tangible legacy projects framed with humility.

notable_anecdotes.description: Self-types emails, speeches, and columns on his desktop; uses MacBook Pro, iPad Pro, and iPhone 12 for online meetings; plays tennis and golf because 'tapping on the keys coordinates my fingers with my mental processes, and walloping tennis and golf balls aligns my eyesight with my nervous system and muscles.'

one_paragraph_summary: Writing 10 days after his second Moderna jab from the Cardinal Santos-Meralco Corporate Wellness Center, in the midst of the Delta-variant lockdown that crushed his hopes of 17 months of 'house arrest' ending, CJ Panganiban offers a personal essay structured by the dyad in his title -- age gracefully, learn endlessly. The 'gracefully' half draws on a Couples for Christ lecture by his high-school chum and brilliant psychiatrist Dr. Cornelio Banaag Jr.: aging has a genetic ceiling but is shaped by manageable factors; socialize online via Viber/WhatsApp to release endorphins; the brain's billions of cells are wired by neurotransmitters that grow with use ('use it or lose it,' 'old dogs can still learn new tricks'); telomeres at chromosome ends function as cell-division clocks shortened by toxic stress and leading to dementia. He grounds the framework in his own family longevity data -- father died at 54, mother at 61, but eldest sister at 90, elder brother at 88, another sister still alive at 88, himself 84 and turning 85 in December -- and credits nutrition, sleep, doctors, medicine, and lifestyle for 'overtaking' heredity. The 'endlessly' half is autobiographical: instead of his planned retreat to a Tagaytay farm, tycoons (mostly previously unmet) recruited him as independent director and adviser, philanthropic/legal/economic/religious groups enlisted him, and he is now 'as busy as when I was in the Court.' He carries judicial independence into corporate directorship ('fidelity to the corporations... not to the owners'); enumerates with evident pride the corporate-finance and technology vocabulary he has acquired post-retirement (CCNI, O&M, NIAT, QoQ, EPS, kWh, GLA, PFRS, US GAAP, DU, WESM; 5G, cloud, OLT, AI, sustainability, blockchain, bitcoin, CX centricity, fintech, deep learning, cracks, silos); reports raising P200 million to retrofit the Manila Cathedral and setting up FLP scholarships, professorial chairs, and dissertation prizes; personally types emails/speeches/columns on his desktop and uses MacBook Pro, iPad Pro, and iPhone 12 for online meetings; and plays tennis and golf because 'walloping tennis and golf balls aligns my eyesight with my nervous system and muscles.' The piece closes with the signature line: 'I find retirement to be merely a change of tires to embark on new journeys. I hope to age gracefully, work happily, learn endlessly, and pray unceasingly until the Lord calls me to an even more glorious journey in His Kingdom of Eternity.'
